questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Limit at Infinity of a General Polynomial
questions.worked_solution:
We identify the leading term and compute its limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }(4{x}^{5}-7{x}^{3}+2x-9) & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }(4{x}^{5}) \\  & =4\cdot {lim}_{x\to \infty }({x}^{5}) \\  & =\infty \,.\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Computing the Limit at Infinity of a General Polynomial

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Root of a Transformed Exponential Function
questions.worked_solution:
To find the root of $f(x),$  we must solve $f(x)=0:$

$$
3{e}^{x+1}+1=0
$$

First, we isolate the term with the variable exponent by subtracting $1$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{e}^{x+1}+1 & =0 \\ 3{e}^{x+1}+\cancel{1}-\cancel{1} & =0-1 \\ 3{e}^{x+1} & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing both sides of the last equation by $3,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{e}^{x+1} & =-1 \\ {e}^{x+1} & =-\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

This equation does not have any solutions since its left-hand side is always nonnegative, while the right-hand side is negative.

Therefore, $f(x)$ has no roots.

provenance.kp_title: Calculating the Root of a Transformed Exponential Function

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Surface Area of a Polyhedron Given Some Lengths
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14004701/assets/93a2ddce7e46f9855f0dd9ea499ae2762cb4538f844ecf7bed7d15d1669b0815.png)

What is the total surface area of the rectangular prism above if it is $2\,\text{cm}$ long, $3\,\text{cm}$ wide, and $3\,\text{cm}$ tall?
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's consider the net of our plank.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14004701/assets/66836a9004af1cc947cbcd70d99f696dd41eaca76214ca4f45a4e8434a7ec7f2.png)

$$

$$

From the diagram, we have squares and rectangles.

The rectangles are $2\,\text{cm}$ long and $3\,\text{cm}$ high. So, the area of one rectangle is:

$$
\text{Area of the rectangle}=2\times 3=6\,{\text{cm}}^{2}.
$$

The squares has the side equal to $3\,\text{cm}.$ Hence, the area of one square is:

$$
\text{Area of the square}=3\times 3=9\,{\text{cm}}^{2}.
$$

Finally, the surface area of the rectangular prism consists of $4$ rectangles and $2$ squares. 

Therefore, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Surface area} & =4\times (\text{Area of the rectangle})+2\times (\text{Area of the square}) \\  & =4\times 6+2\times 9 \\  & =24+18 \\  & =42\,{\text{cm}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Utilizing the Periodicity Property of the Cotangent Function
questions.problem: If $\operatorname{cot}⁡x=-3$ for some $x$, then find the value of $\operatorname{cot}⁡(x+9\pi ).$
questions.worked_solution:
The period of $y=\operatorname{cot}⁡x$ is $\pi .$ Therefore, for integer $n$ we have

$$
\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\operatorname{cot}⁡(x+n\pi ).
$$

Substituting $n=9$ into the right-hand-side of the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cot}⁡x=\operatorname{cot}⁡(x+9\cdot \pi )=\operatorname{cot}⁡(x+9\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if $\operatorname{cot}⁡x=-3,$ then $\operatorname{cot}⁡(x+9\pi )=-3.$

provenance.kp_title: Utilizing the Periodicity Property of the Cotangent Function

questions.knowledge_point: Solving an Exponential Equation by Factoring
questions.problem:
In **ascending order,** the solutions of the equation ${x}^{2}\cdot {4}^{x+1}+5x\cdot {4}^{x+1}+6\cdot {4}^{x+1}=0$ are

$x=$
{{field-1}}$\,$ and $\,x=$
{{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we factor the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot {4}^{x+1}+5x\cdot {4}^{x+1}+6\cdot {4}^{x+1} & =0 \\ ({x}^{2}+5x+6){4}^{x+1} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We can now apply the zero product property, which states that $ab=0$ if and only if $a=0$ or $b=0.$ This gives us two equations,

$$
{x}^{2}+5x+6=0\,\text{and}\,{4}^{x+1}=0.
$$

We now solve each of these equations separately.

- The equation ${x}^{2}+5x+6=0$ can be factored as

$$
(x+2)(x+3)=0,
$$

which leads to the solutions $x=-3,-2.$

- The equation ${4}^{x+1}=0$ has no solutions because ${4}^{x+1}$ is positive for every real number $x.$

Therefore, in ascending order, the original equation has the solutions 

$$
x=-3\,\text{and}\,x=-2.
$$

provenance.kp_title: Solving an Exponential Equation by Factoring

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Roots of a Transformed Radical Function With an Odd Index
questions.worked_solution:
To find the root of $f(x),$ we must solve $f(x)=0:$

$$
-\sqrt[9]{9-12x}-1=0
$$

We solve this equation by making $x$ the subject, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\sqrt[9]{9-12x}-1 & =0 \\ -\sqrt[9]{9-12x} & =1 \\ \sqrt[9]{9-12x} & =-1 \\ (\sqrt[9]{9-12x})^{9} & =(-1)^{9} \\ 9-12x & =-1 \\ -12x & =-10 \\ x & =\frac{5}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the root of $f(x)$ is $x=\frac{5}{6}.$

provenance.kp_title: Finding the Roots of a Transformed Radical Function With an Odd Index

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Derivative Using the Chain and Quotient Rules
questions.worked_solution:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x)={e}^{3{x}^{2}}$ and the denominator $v(x)=x-2.$

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}(x)=6x{e}^{3{x}^{2}},\,{v}^{′}(x)=1.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $u.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(6x{e}^{3{x}^{2}})(x-2)-({e}^{3{x}^{2}})(1)}{(x-2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3{x}^{2}}(6x(x-2)-1)}{(x-2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(6{x}^{2}-12x-1){e}^{3{x}^{2}}}{(x-2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Calculating a Derivative Using the Chain and Quotient Rules

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Sums and Scalar Multiplication of Vectors
questions.worked_solution:
To compute $3a+2b,$ we just need to perform the required operations with each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}3a+2b & =3\cdot ⟨1,-2,0⟩+2\cdot ⟨1,-3,-2⟩ \\  & =⟨3,-6,0⟩+⟨2,-6,-4⟩ \\  & =⟨5,-12,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$
